met_env_water.label: Drinking water quality
met_env_water.suffix: of people are exposed to violations
met_env_water.definition: Three-year average of the percentage of the population getting water from public water systems with at least one health-based violation in the previous year; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the three-year average of the percentage of the population receiving water from public water systems with at least one health-based violation in the previous year.

There are approximately 50,000 regulated drinking water systems that serve water to the same people year-round, referred to as Community Water Systems (CWSs). In FY 2022, 43.2 percent of the nation’s CWSs violated at least one drinking water standard. Additionally, there were monitoring and reporting violations at more than 29.6 percent of CWSs, and health-based violations at 7 percent of CWSs.
met_env_water.map_legend: Avg. % of people exposed to water quality violations
met_env_water.map_title: Avg. % of people exposed to water quality violations
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

We need water to survive, so it’s only natural that livable communities provide residents with clean drinking water. Contaminated drinking water can cause severe health issues ranging from minor discomfort to cancer, kidney damage, nervous system issues, and other life-threatening conditions. This indicator measures how many people receive water from public systems that pose health risks either because there are unacceptable levels of contaminants or disinfectants in the water or because water is inadequately treated. Water quality issues can also indicate that water infrastructure is out-of-date or inadequate to support growth.
met_env_water.results_comparable: No. The methodology changed in 2025, shifting from a 1-year value to a 3-year average.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency Safe Drinking Water Information System, 2023

met_engage_broad.label: Broadband cost and speed
met_engage_broad.suffix: of residents have high-speed, competitively priced service
met_engage_broad.definition: Percentage of residents who have access to three or more wireline or satellite internet service providers, and two or more providers that offer maximum advertised download speeds of at least 100 megabits per second, as well as maximum advertised upload speeds of at least 20 megabits per second; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the percentage of people in a neighborhood who have access to internet service that meets our criteria for both cost and speed, because high-quality internet service should be affordable and fast. In communities that have access to three or more wireline or satellite internet service providers, competition keeps prices down; and where multiple providers offer maximum advertised upload speeds of at least 20 megabits per second and maximum advertised download speeds of at least 100 megabits per second, residents have a variety of affordable options for high-speed service.
met_engage_broad.map_legend: % of residents with access to high-speed, competitively priced service
met_engage_broad.map_title: % of residents with access to high-speed, competitively priced service
missing_data:
__HTML__:

We only assign values to block groups with internet service that meets our criteria for cost and speed. 

It is important to note that not all states report updated data to the National Broadband Map each data release.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The internet isn’t just an option, it’s a necessity. Internet service is crucial in helping a community stay informed and connected, and it opens up new channels for businesses to grow. The Livability Index measures the percentage of people in a neighborhood who have access to internet service that meets our criteria for both cost and speed, because high-quality internet service should be affordable and fast. In communities that have access to three or more wireline or satellite internet service providers, competition keeps prices down; and where multiple providers offer maximum advertised upload speeds of at least 20 megabits per second and maximum advertised download speeds of at least 100 megabits per second, residents have a variety of affordable options for high-speed service.
met_engage_broad.results_comparable: No. The Federal Communications Commission has continually improved its data collection methods since 2015. Omissions in earlier years may not reflect a lack of service.
source: Federal Communications Commission, 2024 Fixed Broadband Deployment Data

met_prox_market.label: Access to grocery stores and farmers' markets
met_prox_market.definition: Number of grocery stores and farmers' markets within a half mile; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Convenience stores are excluded. This metric is calculated by counting the number of grocery stores and farmers’ markets within a one-half mile walking distance from the neighborhood population center. Values at higher levels of geography (e.g., city, county, zip code) represent the average number of grocery stores and farmers’ markets of all neighborhoods within that geography. It does not represent the total number of grocery stores and farmers’ markets within the community.
met_prox_market.map_legend: Number of grocery stores and farmers' markets within a half-mile
met_prox_market.map_title: Number of grocery stores and farmers' markets within a half-mile
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

It’s hard to make healthy food choices if grocery stores and farmers’ markets aren’t nearby. People living in low-income households and individuals who don’t drive are more likely to rely on nearby food sources—and may end up paying more if their only grocery option is a convenience store. Farmers’ markets can also serve as important community gathering places. The Index gives higher scores to communities that provide a wide variety of healthy food options within walking distance.
source: Grocery store locations come from Dun & Bradstreet private data, November 2024;
Farmers’ market locations come from the U.S. Department of Agriculture, Agricultural Marketing Service, Farmers’ Market Directory, November 2024

met_health_smoke.label: Smoking prevalence
met_health_smoke.definition: Estimated smoking rate; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform examines livability by measuring the percentage of adults in a neighborhood who regularly smoke.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data are unavailable for less than 1 percent of neighborhoods. Most of these neighborhoods (2,083 Census block groups) had zero population; hence, their metric value was set to 0.  The remaining 113 Census block groups had non-zero populations and were imputed a metric value set to the county-level value.
rationale:
__HTML__:

As the leading cause of preventable death in the U.S., tobacco not only harms smokers—causing cancer, lung disease, heart disease, and numerous other ailments—but also puts others at risk through secondhand exposure.
met_health_smoke.results_comparable: No. Data source information has changed since 2015.
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Places, 2024

met_opp_income.label: Income inequality
met_opp_income.definition: The Gini Index or coefficient is a measure of income inequality (the gap between rich and poor); lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures how well income is distributed within a county. The Gini coefficient measures how income is distributed across households and is one of the most-used measures of income inequality.  

The Gini coefficient is a number between 0 and 1, with 0 representing perfect equality (i.e., each household has the same amount of income) and 1 representing perfect inequality (i.e., all income is earned by a single household). Income inequality is related to nearly every other category in the AARP Livability Index™ platform, particularly community, neighborhood, housing, and health. In particular, income inequality can lead to reduced longevity and other negative health outcomes and to fewer prospects for long-term economic gains. 

Although data are available at the neighborhood level, we use county-level data to better capture inequalities among neighborhoods within a county.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Using the Gini coefficient, where 0 represents complete equality (every household earns the same income) and 1 represents complete inequality (a single household earns all the income and other households earn nothing), the AARP Livability Index™ platform measures how well income is distributed within a county.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The gap between rich and poor is growing wider across the United States. Higher levels of inequality within a community mean fewer opportunities for low- and middle-income residents to advance, which can lead to a shorter life and greater health problems in the long run.
met_opp_income.results_comparable: Yes. However, the Census Bureau revised the wording of a question on the American Community Survey starting with the 2019 estimates, resulting in an increase in both the number of households reporting retirement income and higher aggregate retirement income at the national level. Please exercise caution when comparing the 2015 metric value, which is based on the 2011–2015 ACS 5-Year Estimates, to current metric values that use more recent ACS estimates incorporating this change.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates

met_trans_freq.label: Frequency of local transit service
met_trans_freq.definition: Total number of buses and trains per hour in both directions for all stops within a quarter-mile; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This metric provides a basis for looking at the overall quality of transit service in a neighborhood by describing the peak frequency of transit service across all stations and stops that are located within walking distance of a neighborhood. The metric counts the total number of bus stops and train stations in both directions during the evening rush hour (4–7pm) within a quarter mile of the neighborhood population center. February 2020 data were used as available to avoid a potential COVID effect in later data feeds.

Data are available only for areas where transit agencies make their route and schedule data publicly available in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format.

A large share of peak-period trips are commute trips, so this metric implicitly focuses on working households, but is also relevant to nonworking households, since in most cases, neighborhoods with more frequent peak service also have more frequent off-peak service.
met_trans_freq.map_legend: Total number of buses and trains per hour in both directions for all stops within a quarter-mile
met_trans_freq.map_title: Total number of buses and trains per hour in both directions for all stops within a quarter-mile
missing_data:
__HTML__:

We do not have data for more than half (52.5 percent) of neighborhoods in the U.S., either because they are not served by public transportation, are only served by demand-responsive services and thus are not captured in the source dataset, or because the transit agency has failed to publicly share its data in the (GTFS) format.

We assign these blocks groups a value of zero, in part to encourage all agencies to share their data with potential customers.
rationale:
__HTML__:

People are far more likely to hop on a bus or train if it’s convenient to their home—and their schedule.
met_trans_freq.results_comparable: No. The source data methodology has changed since 2015.
source: The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s (EPA) and U.S. General Services Administration (GSA) Smart Location Database (SLD), version 3.0, June 2021

met_house_access_step.label: Zero-step entrances
met_house_access_step.definition: Percentage of housing units with a zero-step entrance; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Residences that can be entered without a step are assessed in each biennial round of the American Housing Survey (AHS) and are a key accessibility feature. The survey assesses 25 metropolitan areas every release year. Fifteen of these areas are sampled each release year and 10 of them are selected from a rotating sample of twenty metropolitan areas. The platform also uses data from 16 additional metropolitan areas taken from the AHS predating 2015. 
Other residential features (e.g., extra-wide doors or hallways, entry-level bedrooms and bathrooms, and floors without steps between rooms) are important for measuring accessibility at home; however, they are not assessed regularly by the U.S. Census Bureau and thus are not included in this AARP Livability Index™ metric.
met_house_access_step.map_legend: Avg. % of housing units with zero-step entry
met_house_access_step.map_title: Avg. % of housing units with zero-step entry
missing_data:
__HTML__:

About half of U.S. neighborhoods are located outside metropolitan areas. These neighborhoods are imputed with the state average.  
Where neither metro area nor state-level data are available, we impute with the national average (56.1 percent)
Earlier data vintages are used when 2023 data were unavailable for a given metro area. Because of this, caution is advised when comparing locations.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The majority of Americans want to stay in their homes as they age. Many will host guests or have older family members with restricted mobility. It’s desirable to have a home that’s both accessible and aesthetically pleasing. Functional, tasteful designs that enable anyone to enter the home—by foot, wheelchair, or walker—constitutes accessible housing. Here, the Index assesses the percentage of housing units that can be entered without steps.
met_house_access_step.results_comparable: No. The metric was redefined in 2018 to improve data coverage and better estimate accessibility. It was further refined in 2022 to use historic data where available.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2023 American Housing Survey

met_health_obese.label: Obesity prevalence
met_health_obese.definition: Estimated obesity rate; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the percentage of adults in a neighborhood who are obese, adjusted for age.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data are unavailable for less than 1 percent of neighborhoods. Most of these neighborhoods (2,083 Census block groups) had zero population; hence, their metric value was set to 0. The remaining 113 Census block groups had non-zero populations and were imputed a metric value set to the county-level value.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Second only to tobacco use as the leading cause of preventable death in the U.S., obesity directly causes heart disease, diabetes, and high blood pressure. High obesity rates can indicate that a community lacks access to healthy food or exercise opportunities.
met_health_obese.results_comparable: No. Data source information has changed since 2015.
source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Places, 2024

met_house_multifam.label: Availability of multi-family housing
met_house_multifam.definition: Percentage of housing units that are not single-family, detached homes; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Livable communities offer housing for any situation, which is why the AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the percentage of housing units in a community that are not single-family, detached homes.
met_house_multifam.map_legend: % of housing units that aren't single-family detached
met_house_multifam.map_title: % of housing units that aren't single-family detached
missing_data:
__HTML__:

We assigned zeroes to 2,646 Census block groups that have zero total housing units.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The majority of U.S. homes are single-family, detached houses that are often well-suited for larger households, such as families with children. Sometimes referred to as “missing middle housing,” townhouses, condominiums, apartments or duplexes often meet the household needs of older adults in certain situations, such as those whose children have moved out or have a deceased spouse. This type of housing is also often preferred by single-parent families, childless couples or those who choose to live with a roommate.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates

met_opp_jobs.label: Jobs per worker
met_opp_jobs.definition: Number of jobs per person in the workforce; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform examines the number of jobs per worker in metropolitan areas, micropolitan areas, and other areas within states. Communities that have at least one job per worker have a value of 1; places where there are fewer jobs than workers receive lower values.

Values are capped at 1.0 job per person in the workforce because values above 1 can be a sign that a metropolitan area, micropolitan area, or other areas in states with a strong economy are not providing enough housing to accommodate workers.
met_opp_jobs.map_legend: Number of jobs per person in the workforce
met_opp_jobs.map_title: Number of jobs per person in the workforce
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Missing value for Kalawao County, HI, was imputed with the value for Maui County, HI.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The more job options that metropolitan, micropolitan, or other areas within states offer, the more selective residents can be in their search for employment. However, when that ratio reverses and citizens outnumber open positions, people are forced to consider jobs that are less fulfilling and possibly farther away.
met_opp_jobs.scale: Metro area scale, other areas within a state
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2023 Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics data

met_engage_civic.label: Opportunity for civic involvement
met_engage_civic.definition: Number of civic, social, religious, political, and business organizations per 10,000 people; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures how well a county is served by civic, social, religious, and business organizations.

Available data captures only institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations.
met_engage_civic.map_legend: Number of civic, social, religious, political, and business organizations per 10,000 people
met_engage_civic.map_title: Number of civic, social, religious, political, and business organizations per 10,000 people
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Available data captures only institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Strong communities give residents plenty of opportunities to work together and effect change. Whether it’s a fundraiser, election, or volunteer event, nothing helps bring a neighborhood together like civic participation. These events, and the organizations that facilitate them, give like-minded people a chance to meet and make a difference. The Livability Index measures how well a county is served by civic organizations. Available data captures only cultural institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations.
met_engage_civic.results_comparable: No. Data sources and methodology have changed since 2015.
source: Dun & Bradstreet private data, November 2024 [private data]

met_env_air.label: Regional air quality
met_env_air.suffix: unhealthy air quality days per year
met_env_air.definition: Number of days per year when regional air quality is unhealthy for sensitive populations; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the number of days per year when a county’s AQI score is 101 or higher, using three years of data and controlling for year-to-year changes in the weather. For areas that don’t report air quality data, we assume the national average.
met_env_air.map_legend: Number of days per year with unhealthy air quality
met_env_air.map_title: Number of days per year with unhealthy air quality
missing_data:
__HTML__:

For block groups where only one or two years were missing data, we assigned the block group the average of the year(s) with available data. For block groups where all three years were missing data, we assigned the national average for block groups in counties that do report data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Poor air quality not only makes day-to-day life less enjoyable but also poses long-term health threats, especially for young people, older adults, and people who are at risk of developing asthma and other respiratory diseases. The Air Quality Index (AQI) measures the level of several different air pollutants on a scale of 0 to 500. An AQI of 101 or higher is considered unhealthy for sensitive populations.
met_env_air.results_comparable: No. Data may not be comparable with years prior to the 2023 release for highly polluted locations as previous versions may not have included "hazardous" in the calculation.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 2021-2023 Air Quality Index Report

met_prox_park.label: Access to parks
met_prox_park.definition: Number of parks within a half-mile; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This metric is calculated by counting the number of city, county, state, and national parks within a one-half mile walking distance from the neighborhood population center.

A wide variety of park types are included, provided that there is no barrier to entry for any portion of the population (i.e., parks, trails, and school playgrounds governed by joint-use agreements, and privately owned parks managed for public use).

Values at higher levels of geography (e.g., city, county, zip code) represent the average number of parks in neighborhoods within that geography. It does not represent the total number of parks within the community.
met_prox_park.map_legend: Number of parks within a half-mile
met_prox_park.map_title: Number of parks within a half-mile
missing_data:
__HTML__:

 No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Parks provide opportunities for people to exercise, gather with friends, or simply enjoy the outdoors. It’s no wonder that most people surveyed by AARP value having a park within walking distance. Communities with multiple nearby parks may provide greater access to trails, athletic facilities, picnic tables, playgrounds, and more.
source: Trust for Public Land ParkServe database, May 2024, supplemented by ESRI and OpenStreetsMap data

met_trans_access.label: ADA-accessible stations and vehicles
met_trans_access.suffix: of stations and vehicles are accessible
met_trans_access.definition: Percentage of transit stations and vehicles that are ADA-accessible; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform examines the percentage of transit stations and vehicles in metropolitan areas that are wheelchair accessible according to the requirements of the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).  

This metric measures accessibility across a metropolitan area since the system must be accessible at both origin and destination to enable a person with mobility issues to use transit. However, the metric does not indicate whether the approach (e.g., sidewalk) to a bus stop is accessible to someone using a wheelchair.
met_trans_access.map_legend: % of transit stations and vehicles that are ADA-accessible
met_trans_access.map_title: % of transit stations and vehicles that are ADA-accessible
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Neighborhoods with missing data are assigned the rural average for the nation (85.4 percent).
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Transit data for rural areas aren’t quite as detailed as those for urban areas. We estimate accessibility for rural areas by calculating the average of accessibility data submitted by rural transit agencies across the United States (85.4%).
rationale:
__HTML__:

People with restricted mobility rely heavily on convenient public transit equipped with accessible features, such as buses with wheelchair ramps and stations with elevators. In addition to allowing wheelchair users to enjoy the transit system, accessible stations and vehicles can also make it easier for people with other mobility issues to use transit. Advanced age alone does not qualify individuals to use paratransit services required by the ADA.
source: Federal Transit Administration, 2023 National Transit Database

met_env_road.label: Near-roadway pollution
met_env_road.suffix: of people are exposed to near-roadway pollution
met_env_road.definition: Percentage of the population living within 200 meters of a high-traffic road with more than 25,000 vehicles per day; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the percentage of people in a neighborhood who live close enough to high-traffic roads that they are regularly exposed to these negative impacts.

The majority of block groups (63.3 percent) do not contain any people who live near a high-traffic roadway, so those with even a small share of their population living within 200 meters of a high-traffic road perform poorly with respect to this metric. Any exposure to near-roadway pollution should be cause for concern.
met_env_road.map_legend: % of the population living within 200 meters of a high-traffic road with more than 25,000 vehicles per day
met_env_road.map_title: % of the population living within 200 meters of a high-traffic road with more than 25,000 vehicles per day
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

A high-traffic road isn’t just a nuisance to navigate - it can be a threat to public health, too. People who live near these roads are exposed to stressful noise pollution, not to mention exhaust and other emissions that can increase the risk of cancer and asthma. Busy roads also create barriers for pedestrians and bicyclists.
met_env_road.results_comparable: No. Results of this analysis should not be compared over time due to changes in state data collection methods.
source: Highway Performance Monitoring System (HPMS), provided by the Federal Highway Administration (FHWA)

met_house_cost.label: Housing costs
met_house_cost.definition: Average monthly housing costs per household; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Average monthly housing costs are capped at $4,000. The AARP Livability Index™ platform accounts for housing costs (including taxes, rent, mortgage fees, and utilities) existing residents pay to help users compare the costs of living in different neighborhoods. It does not reflect the market-rate price to rent or buy in the current local housing market.
met_house_cost.map_legend: Avg. monthly housing cost, per household
met_house_cost.map_title: Avg. monthly housing cost, per household
missing_data:
__HTML__:

In neighborhoods where there are no recorded housing units, we assign the national average monthly housing cost and mark these as imputed. The national average monthly housing cost is $1,464.29.

Beginning with the 2022 update of the AARP Livability Index™ platform, when data are not available at the neighborhood level (Census block group), we use higher levels of geography (Census tract, county, or, as a last resort, state-level data). As such, comparisons to 2015 data are not appropriate for only a small minority of neighborhoods.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform accounts for housing costs (including taxes, rent, mortgage fees, and utilities) that existing residents pay to help users compare the costs of living in different neighborhoods. It does not reflect the market-rate price to rent or buy in the current local housing market.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Housing typically takes the biggest portion of our paycheck or pension and when prices soar, our quality of life suffers. Higher monthly rent or mortgage payments leave less money for food, transportation, and health care, and restrict housing options for many households, including those with fixed or low-to-moderate incomes.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates

met_prox_lib.label: Access to libraries
met_prox_lib.definition: Number of libraries within a half-mile; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The metric is calculated by counting the number of libraries within a one-half mile walking distance from the neighborhood population center.  

Values at higher levels of geography (e.g., city, county, zip code) represent the average number of libraries of all neighborhoods within that geography. It does not represent the total number of libraries within the community.
met_prox_lib.map_legend: Number of libraries within a half-mile
met_prox_lib.map_title: Number of libraries within a half-mile
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the number of libraries within walking distance of a neighborhood, capping values at 1 since few neighborhoods have more than one library.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Libraries promote literacy, provide internet access and other services, and serve as community gathering spaces. They can be particularly important for low-income residents, who may lack the money to purchase books or internet access at home.
source: Institute of Museum and Library Services, 2022 Public Libraries Survey

met_engage_vote.label: Voting rate
met_engage_vote.definition: Percentage of people ages 18 years or older who voted in the last presidential election; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform uses data from the most recent presidential election.

Results are bound at 30 percent and 85 percent to address intrinsic outliers resulting from using two different data sources (voting data from Dave Leip's Election Atlas and population data from the latest ACS population estimates).
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Voting is one of the simplest—and strongest—ways we can show we care about our communities. People who vote in national elections are more likely to also be politically informed and active on a local level, participating in local elections that directly shape community life. Low participation may reflect voting barriers within a community.
met_engage_vote.results_comparable: No. Data source and methodology has changed since 2015.
source: Dave Leip's Atlas of U.S. Elections, 2024 Presidential Election Results by County

met_trans_walk.label: Walkability index
met_trans_walk.definition: Relative walkability of a neighborhood compared to all other neighborhoods in the U.S.; higher values are better on a scale of 1 to 20
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform pulls walkability data directly from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s National Walkability Index, where: 

  • 1 - 5.75 = Least Walkable

  • 5.76 - 10.50 = Below Average Walkable

  • 10.51 - 15.25 = Above Average Walkable

  • 15.26 - 20 = Most Walkable

Neighborhoods are assessed based on measures known to influence the likelihood of people walking as a means of transportation: street intersection density,  proximity to transit stops, and diversity of land uses.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Walkability includes factors known to influence the likelihood of people walking, such as proximity to transit stops and how easy it is to navigate local streets.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Walkable neighborhoods offer a multitude of benefits to residents and the community as a whole. They encourage more physical activity, leading to improved health and longevity. They enable residents and workers to drive less, thus cutting down on pollution and noise. Additionally, walkable neighborhoods promote social interaction and a sense of community, as people are more likely to encounter their neighbors and friends when walking for exercise or to nearby services and amenities.
met_trans_walk.results_comparable: No. The metric definition and data source have changed in 2023.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) National Walkability Index

met_opp_grad.label: High school graduation rate
met_opp_grad.suffix: of students graduating within four years
met_opp_grad.definition: Adjusted 4-year high school cohort graduation rate; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform looks at the likelihood that a student entering a local public high school will graduate within four years. This metric is measured at the school level where data are available, otherwise at the school district level.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Census block groups with missing data are assigned the corresponding state-level average. Block groups that use school district data instead of school-level data are not considered to be imputed.
rationale:
__HTML__:

In the face of today’s hypercompetitive career and college landscape, it’s crucial for youth to have access to high-quality education that keeps them supported and motivated from kindergarten through high school. By looking at a community’s high school graduation rates, we can gauge the quality of the local educational system as a whole.
met_opp_grad.results_comparable: No. The methodology has changed since 2015. Most data are not comparable. Some graduation rates are masked with a range based on the size of a school's graduating class population. The magnitudes of the ranges decrease as the size of the graduating class population increases. Small population changes can result in large (artificial) changes in graduation rates.
source: U.S. Department of Education, ED Data Express, School Year 2021-2022 Four-Year Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rates

met_health_exercise.label: Access to exercise opportunities
met_health_exercise.definition: Percentage of people who live within a half mile of parks and within 1 mile of recreational facilities (3 miles for rural areas); higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the percentage of people in a county who live reasonably close to both parks and recreational facilities, accounting for the fact that people in rural areas may be willing to travel farther to exercise.

Individuals are considered to have access to exercise opportunities if they reside:  

  • in a census block that is within a half mile of a park 

  • in an urban census block that is within one mile of a recreational facility 

  • in a rural census block that is within three miles of a recreational facility

Parks include local, state, and national parks. Recreational facilities include YMCAs as well as businesses, including a wide variety of facilities such as gyms, community centers, dance studios, and pools.
met_health_exercise.map_legend: % of people with access to exercise opportunities
met_health_exercise.map_title: % of people with access to exercise opportunities
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data were missing for 52 counties in the CHR dataset based on 2019 counties. For 43 of these, we used 2024 state-level data for exercise opportunities, as they were missing values in both 2023 and 2024 CHR data, and flagged them as imputed. For the remaining counties, we used 2023 county data from the same data source, and did NOT flag as imputed.

Lastly, we imputed zero population Census Block Groups with zero values and labeled them as imputed. We obtained CBG population counts from ACS Total Population (table B01003) 5-year estimates for 2019-2023.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Physical activity doesn’t just help people get in shape, it also reduces the risk of medical conditions such as obesity, diabetes, cancer, and dementia. Easy access to parks and recreational facilities such as gyms and community centers not only makes residents more likely to exercise, but also creates a sense of community, since these locations often double as meeting places.
met_health_exercise.results_comparable: No. Data sources and methodology have changed since 2015.
source: Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute, 2024 & 2023 County Health Rankings & Roadmaps

met_engage_social.label: Social involvement index
met_engage_social.definition: Extent to which residents belong to groups, organizations, or associations, see or hear from friends and family, do favors for neighbors, or do something positive for their community; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Using the Volunteering and Civic Life Supplement of the Current Population Survey, AARP calculates an indexed metric based on four survey questions:  

  1. In the past 12 months, how often did you talk to or spend time with friends and family? 

  1. How often did you and your neighbors do favors for each other, such as house sitting, watching each other’s children, lending tools, and other things to help each other? 

  1. Did you get together with other people from your neighborhood to do something positive for your neighborhood or the community? 

  2. Did you belong to any groups, organizations, or associations?

Communities where people socialize and participate in civic-minded activity more frequently than average receive values above 1; those with people who do so less frequently receive values below 1.

Data are available for 260 metropolitan areas. For neighborhoods outside of these areas, we use state-level data.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Being neighborly isn’t just a matter of etiquette—it’s what creates a community, often with lasting benefits for its residents. In fact, studies show that Americans who socialize regularly live longer. Here, using data at the metro level for the select 260 metropolitan areas and state-level data for other places, we look at how often people interact with their friends and neighbors. Communities where people socialize more frequently than average receive values above 1; those with people who socialize less frequently receive values below 1.
met_engage_social.results_comparable: No. In 2017, the Volunteering and Civic Life Supplements were combined and some questions dropped or reworded, thus results are not comparable with previous years.
source: U.S. Census Bureau Current Population Survey, September 2023: Volunteering and Civic Life Supplement, conducted for the Corporation for National and Community Service

met_opp_age.label: Age diversity
met_opp_age.definition: Age-group diversity of local population compared to the national population; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform compares local age diversity to the national age distribution using three age groups: children (ages 0–14), working-age teenagers and adults (ages 15–54), and experienced workers and people who are retired (ages 55+). Values range from 0 to 1. Communities that mirror the national age distribution receive a value of 1, while communities that are least similar to the national age distribution receive a value of 0. The typical neighborhood in the U.S. is less diverse than the nation as a whole. This is reflected in the median U.S. neighborhood showing a value of 0.83.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Neighborhoods with missing values are assigned a value of 1 on the final scale.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Communities that mirror the national age distribution receive a value of 1, while communities that are least similar to the national age distribution receive a value of 0. The typical neighborhood in the United States is less diverse than the nation as a whole, as reflected in the median U.S. neighborhood showing a value of 0.83.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Multigenerational communities are ripe with opportunities for residents to learn from and support each other in meaningful ways, from formal interactions like tutoring or computer classes to spontaneous encounters on the bus, at the grocery store, or at places of worship. People at different phases of life contribute to the economy and well-being of the community in many different ways, including by working, paying taxes, supporting local businesses, and volunteering. A lack of age diversity may signify a community that is unaffordable or socially isolating.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates

met_prox_trans.label: Access to jobs by transit
met_prox_trans.definition: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute transit commute; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute commute by transit, giving more credit to nearby jobs than those farther away.  

February 2020 pre-COVID-19 transit data are used where available. 

Data are available only for areas where transit agencies make their route and schedule data publicly available in the General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS format).
met_prox_trans.map_legend: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute transit commute
met_prox_trans.map_title: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute transit commute
missing_data:
__HTML__:

About 60 percent of U.S. neighborhoods show no transit service, either because there is no regular bus or rail service, there is only demand-responsive services not captured in the data, or because the transit agency has not shared its routes and schedule data with the (GTF) system.  

We assign these neighborhoods a value of zero, in part to encourage all agencies to share their data with potential customers.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The platform measures the number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute commute by transit, giving more credit to nearby jobs than those farther away. Note: Data are available only for areas where transit agencies make their route and schedule data publicly available in the  General Transit Feed Specification (GTFS) format.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Millions of commuters use buses, trains, and subways each day to get to work. For these workers, convenient and dependable transit isn’t just a perk—it’s a necessity. Good public transportation generally costs less than driving and parking, encourages more walking, and reduces air pollution. Better accessibility means residents have more job options within a reasonable commute by public transportation.
met_prox_trans.results_comparable: No. Source methodology has changed since 2015.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Smart Location Database, version 3.0, June 2021. Note: EPA used February 2020 pre-COVID-19 transit data where available.

met_trans_delay.label: Congestion
met_trans_delay.definition: Estimated total hours that the average person spends in traffic each year; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform looks at the total amount of time per year that the average person in an urban area spends sitting in traffic.

Since congestion affects people’s access to destinations across the entire transportation system, this metric is measured at the metropolitan area scale. There are many congestion metrics used in transportation planning; this metric looks at delay throughout the day instead of focusing on rush hour, so it captures congestion’s impact on all trips (e.g., mid-day medical appointments in addition to travel to and from work).

We control for population growth to highlight how congestion changes over time due to transportation policy and investment rather than population growth.

We assume that rural areas experience no vehicle delays. While congestion is indeed negligible in many rural areas, this assumption likely leads the platform to underestimate delay in rural areas immediately adjacent to urban areas that experience spillover congestion.
met_trans_delay.map_legend: Estimated total hours that the average person spends in traffic each year
met_trans_delay.map_title: Estimated total hours that the average person spends in traffic each year
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data are missing for about 33 percent of neighborhoods (those located outside urbanized areas). These neighborhoods were assigned a metric value of 0.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform looks at the total amount of time per year that the average person in an urban area spends sitting in traffic. Due to the lack of data for rural areas, we assume such areas do not experience congestion.
rationale:
__HTML__:

From a bustling economy to a vibrant culture, some communities have it all, but traffic congestion could make it hard for residents to enjoy these amenities. Not only do clogged roads wreck schedules and make appealing destinations hard to reach, they also increase air pollution. Here, the platform looks at the total amount of time per year that the average person in an urban area spends sitting in traffic. Due to the lack of data for rural areas, we assume such areas do not experience congestion.
met_trans_delay.results_comparable: No. The data source changed its calculation methods since 2015.
source: Texas Transportation Institute 2023 Urban Mobility Report (2022 data).

met_health_short.label: Healthcare professional shortage areas
met_health_short.definition: Severity of clinician shortage; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

In order to target health care resources to communities in need, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services identifies Health Professional Shortage Areas (HPSAs) based on the ratio of primary care clinicians to the population, poverty levels, infant health, and travel time to the nearest accessible care location. About 25 percent of the U.S. population resides in primary medical care HPSAs. Each HPSA receives a clinician priority score ranging from 0 to 25 that indicates how high of a priority it is to assign health professionals to the area, with 25 indicating the highest priority (i.e., highest level of shortage).
met_health_short.map_legend: Health Professional Shortage Area score (Index from 0 to 25)
met_health_short.map_title: Health Professional Shortage Area score (Index from 0 to 25)
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Areas of the country not in the dataset are located outside HPSAs and are assigned a zero value.
rationale:
__HTML__:

It is difficult for residents of areas with inadequate numbers of health care professionals to access preventive care, which can increase travel distances and the cost of care. People with poor access may avoid the preventive care that could reduce their risk of developing more serious health conditions. The impact may be most extreme for low-income people who cannot afford the cost it would take to travel for health care.
met_health_short.results_comparable: Partially - on GEOIDs that remained mostly the same
source: Health Resources and Services Administration, Health Professional Shortage Area Data, August 2024

met_env_pollute.label: Local industrial pollution
met_env_pollute.definition: Toxicity of airborne chemicals released from nearby industrial facilities; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform assesses health impacts from all major industrial pollution sources within 1,000 feet of a neighborhood using a tool that measures relative health risks from different pollutants. This conservative buffer is used to capture air pollution that travels by wind to nearby polluters.  

More than 90 percent of U.S. neighborhoods have no local industrial pollution and receive a score of zero. On the other hand, communities with trace amounts of pollution perform poorly on this metric. Any local pollution should be cause for concern.  

Since some pollutants produce greater adverse health effects than others, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency weighs each pollutant independently according to its relative toxicity, routes of exposure, and likely dosage. Risk-Screening Environmental Indicators (RSEI) toxicity weights are based on human health effects associated with long-term exposure to chemicals.
met_env_pollute.map_legend: Toxicity of airborne chemicals released from nearby industrial facilities
met_env_pollute.map_title: Toxicity of airborne chemicals released from nearby industrial facilities
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

A Risk-Screening Environmental Indicators (RSEI) Score is a unitless value that accounts for the size of the chemical release, the fate and transport of the chemical through the environment, the size and location of the exposed population, and the chemical’s toxicity. RSEI Scores range from 0 to 10,757.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Industrial facilities emit a wide range of pollutants that taint the local air and damage the health and quality of life for nearby residents, especially older adults, children, and those who have difficulty breathing.
met_env_pollute.results_comparable: No. RSEI weights for each chemical are relative to other chemicals on a list, which changes with new statutory requirements. As such, a given chemical can have a different weight in different years, leading to large variations in results.
source: The location of sources and type of pollution come from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s 2023 Toxic Release Inventory
The toxicity of pollutants comes from EPA’s 2024 Risk-Screening Environmental Indicators model

met_house_burden.label: Housing cost burden
met_house_burden.definition: Percentage of income devoted to monthly housing costs; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform assesses housing cost burden based on average living expenses and income in a neighborhood.   

Housing costs include taxes, rent, mortgage fees, and utilities that existing residents pay to help users compare the costs of living in different  neighborhoods.
met_house_burden.map_legend: Avg. % of household income spent on housing
met_house_burden.map_title: Avg. % of household income spent on housing
missing_data:
__HTML__:

In neighborhoods where there are no recorded housing units (2,691 Census block groups), we assign the national average and mark these as imputed. Additionally, 40 Census Block Groups in New York are missing data in the ACS dataset due to data collection errors in some New York locations - namely cases of incorrect geocoding in Watchtower, and problems occurring during data collection in Wyandanch CDP and Brentwood CDP (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/errata/147.html and https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/errata/148.html). They have been imputed with their metric values from the v2024 release.

Beginning with the 2022 version of the platform, when data are not available at the neighborhood level (Census block group), we use higher levels of geography (Census tract, county, or as a last resort, state-level data). As such, comparisons to 2015 data are not appropriate for a small minority of neighborhoods.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform compares neighborhood housing costs (including taxes, rent, mortgage fees, and utilities) to average incomes in the greater metropolitan area or county.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Bigger cities may offer more and higher-paying employment opportunities, but often have higher housing costs, as well. Ideally, big-city salaries are adequate to cover both housing and other living expenses. Here, the Index compares neighborhood housing costs to average incomes in the greater metropolitan area or county.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimate
United States Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD)

met_prox_auto.label: Access to jobs by auto
met_prox_auto.definition: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute automobile commute; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This metric measures the number of jobs within a 45-minute drive of a given neighborhood, weighting jobs by distance so that nearby jobs receive higher value.
met_prox_auto.map_legend: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute automobile commute
met_prox_auto.map_title: Number of jobs accessible within a 45-minute automobile commute
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Automobiles are the primary mode of travel in the U.S. and are necessary in areas with insufficient transit service. Better accessibility means less time sitting in the car, less money spent on gas and maintenance, and more time with friends and family. Commuting to work represents a significant portion of travel for working households, and the location of jobs can serve as a proxy for the location of other destinations, such as shopping and commercial centers, that are important to both working and nonworking households. Studies have found that increased automobile accessibility corresponds with a reduction in vehicle travel since travelers drive shorter distances to reach destinations.
met_prox_auto.results_comparable: No. Source methodology has changed since 2015.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, Smart Location Database, version 3.0, June 2021

met_house_subsidy.label: Availability of subsidized housing
met_house_subsidy.definition: Number of subsidized housing units per 10,000 people; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

Housing subsidies—government funding for the difference between the market rent and the amount of rent a tenant can afford or for the construction of low-rent units—help people afford to live in otherwise livable communities that have high housing costs. 

The tracked subsidies included in the AARP Livability Index™ platform are HUD rental assistance programs (Section 8, Section 202, Rental Assistance Payments), HUD mortgage insurance programs (Section 236, Section 221), and other federal sources (Section 202 Direct Loans, Low-Income Housing Tax Credits, HOME Rental Assistance, USDA Rural Development Loans).
met_house_subsidy.map_legend: Number of subsidized housing units per 10,000 people
met_house_subsidy.map_title: Number of subsidized housing units per 10,000 people
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data. In neighborhoods that have zero population (2,079 Census block groups), we assign a metric value of zero and mark these as imputed.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Housing and other prices often are higher in more desirable communities. As communities become “hot,” affordable options for low- and moderate-income residents may shrink. Residents with lower incomes are most likely to depend on the access to transit, stores, and jobs that popular communities offer. Subsidized housing helps such residents afford to live in higher-cost communities.
met_house_subsidy.results_comparable: No. Due to an improvement in data collection by the source, the metric moved from a county measure to a neighborhood measure.
source: Public and Affordable Housing Research Corporation and the National Low Income Housing Coalition’s April 2024 National Housing Preservation Database
U.S. Housing and Urban Development (HUD) Public Housing Buildings August 2024 database

met_health_hospital.label: Preventable hospitalization rate
met_health_hospital.definition: Number of hospital admissions for conditions that could be effectively treated through outpatient care per 1,000 patients; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index platform measures how frequently people are hospitalized for conditions that could be treated at a doctor’s office or urgent care clinic to gauge the quality of a community’s health care system outside its hospitals. Hospitalization for asthma, high blood pressure, diabetes, and dehydration is considered preventable. Communities receive a value based on data from nearby hospitals.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

There are 77 counties with missing values for preventable hospitalization in the CHR dataset. For 18 of these counties for which previous-year CHR data exists, we used the earlier vintage (2023). We did not flag these 18 counties as imputed. The remaining 59 counties for which previous-year CHR data doesn't exist were imputed with the state-level values for the states they are located in from the 2024 dataset. These 59 counties were flagged as imputed.

Lastly, we imputed zero population Census Block Groups with zero values and labeled them as imputed. We obtained CBG population counts from ACS Total Population (table B01003) 5-year estimates for 2019-2023.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Some patients occasionally wind up hospitalized with serious conditions that could have been easily prevented with better primary care or patient education. Hospitalization for asthma, high blood pressure, diabetes, and dehydration is considered preventable. Communities receive a value based on data from nearby hospitals.
met_health_hospital.results_comparable: No. Source methodology has changed since 2015.
source: Robert Wood Johnson Foundation and University of Wisconsin Population Health Institute, 2024 & 2023 County Health Rankings & Roadmaps

met_trans_cost.label: Household transportation costs
met_trans_cost.definition: Estimated household transportation costs; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform displays the estimated cost of transportation in different neighborhoods.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development considers housing and transportation costs to be affordable if together they consume no more than 45 percent of a household’s income.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data are missing for less than 1 percent of U.S. neighborhoods. The missing values were imputed with data from broader geographic areas such as cities, counties or states.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Second only to housing in U.S. household spending, transportation can be a significant financial burden, especially for households on a fixed income. Residents who purchase homes in cheaper neighborhoods can wind up paying more for gas and cars if their neighborhood lacks transit, isn’t walkable, or is far from jobs and services. Here, the AARP Livability Index™ platform displays the estimated cost of transportation in different neighborhoods.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Second only to housing in U.S. household spending, transportation can be a significant financial burden, especially for households with lower incomes or on a fixed income. Residents who purchase homes in cheaper neighborhoods can wind up paying more for gas and cars if their neighborhood lacks transit, isn’t walkable, or is far from jobs and services.
source: The Center for Neighborhood Technology's (CNT) Housing and Transportation Affordability Index, 2022 data, downloaded February 2025

met_engage_culture.label: Cultural, arts, and entertainment institutions
met_engage_culture.definition: Number of movie theaters and entertainment centers within 5 miles and performing arts and sports venues within 15 miles per 10,000 people; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The metric measures the concentration of cultural, arts, and entertainment opportunities by providing a per capita number of relevant institutions. This is a commonly used metric to capture the availability of arts and cultural establishments.

Available data captures only institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations, such as community theater groups.

We use statistical techniques to account for extremely high rates in large geographic areas with low population.
met_engage_culture.map_legend: Number of performing arts companies, museums, concert venues, sports stadiums, and movie theaters per 10,000 people
met_engage_culture.map_title: Number of performing arts companies, museums, concert venues, sports stadiums, and movie theaters per 10,000 people
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Available data captures only cultural institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations.
rationale:
__HTML__:

From sports fanatics to film buffs, a great community helps cultivate the interests of its residents through opportunities to learn, play, and interact with others. Here, the Livability Index measures how many cultural, arts, and entertainment institutions serve community residents. Our data capture only cultural institutions with paid staff, not volunteer-run organizations, such as community theater groups.
met_engage_culture.results_comparable: No. Data sources and methodology have changed since 2015.
source: Dun & Bradstreet private data, November 2024 [private data]

met_prox_land_use.label: Diversity of destinations
met_prox_land_use.definition: Mix of jobs within a mile; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures how well a neighborhood offers convenient access to retail, entertainment, health care, education, food, and personal services. This metric is measured on a scale from 0 to 1. Mixed land uses are a key characteristic of livable neighborhoods.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data were missing for 22,498 Census block groups. Data were only reported if there were jobs in the five employment types included in this metric (i.e., retail, entertainment, health care, education, and food or personal services). A metric value of 0 was assigned to Census block groups with missing data and marked as imputed.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The mix of jobs within a mile reflects the likelihood that a variety of destinations and services are available within the neighborhood. Livable neighborhoods make it easy for residents to walk to a diverse range of destinations. 

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures how well a neighborhood offers convenient access to retail, entertainment, health care, education, and food or personal services. Measured on a scale from 0 to 1, higher values are given to communities that offer better access.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The mix of jobs within a mile reflects the likelihood that a variety of destinations and services are available within the neighborhood. Livable neighborhoods make it easy for residents to walk to a diverse range of destinations and services.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2022 Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LEHD LODES)

met_trans_limit.label: Speed limits
met_trans_limit.definition: Average speed limit on streets and highways; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform analyzes average speed limits for all streets in a neighborhood, giving greater weight to streets with more lanes, since wide streets are riskier and more challenging to cross.
met_trans_limit.map_legend: Avg. speed limit (MPH) on streets and highways
met_trans_limit.map_title: Avg. speed limit (MPH) on streets and highways
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The odds that a pedestrian who gets hit by a vehicle will die increase drastically when the car is moving faster than 20 miles per hour. Lower, safer speed limits help residents feel confident walking and biking around their neighborhoods, resulting in healthier people and more vibrant communities. Lower speeds also make travel by cars and trucks safer as well.
met_trans_limit.results_comparable: No. Data sources have been updated to improve data coverage and metric values.
source: Nexar private data, April 2025
U.S. Department of Transportation, Highway Performance Monitoring System, February 2025

met_health_sate.label: Patient satisfaction
met_health_sate.definition: Percentage of patients who give area hospitals a rating of 9 or 10, with 10 indicating the highest level of satisfaction; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to the percentage of patients who give Medicare-certified hospitals a rating of 9 or 10, with 10 indicating the highest level of satisfaction on the Hospital Consumer Assessment Healthcare Providers and Systems (HCAHPS) Patient Survey.

The HCAHPS survey contains patient perspectives on care and patient rating items that encompass key topics: communication with hospital staff, responsiveness of hospital staff, communication about medicines, discharge information, cleanliness of hospital environment, quietness of hospital environment, and transition of care.
met_health_sate.map_legend: % of patients who give area hospitals a rating of 9 or 10
met_health_sate.map_title: % of patients who give area hospitals a rating of 9 or 10
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Neighborhoods with missing data are  imputed with the national average (67.98 percent).
rationale:
__HTML__:

High-quality care produces not only satisfied patients, but also healthier ones. People are less likely to postpone medically necessary hospital care if they were satisfied with their last experience. Obtaining necessary care results in a lower likelihood of developing serious conditions down the road. Patient satisfaction can reflect the overall quality of care people receive in the hospital. Poor quality care can result in readmission, new illness, and other serious adverse outcomes.
met_health_sate.scale: Hospital Service Area (HSA). We take the data of individual hospitals in an HSA (what hospital is in what HSA is determined by the ZIP code of the hospital which is provided in the HCAHPS data). We aggregate the data of all hospitals in an HSA to get the HSA metric value. The HSA metric value is then allocated down to whatever CBGs are in that HSA. HSAs represent local health care markets for hospital care and are defined by the National Center for Health Statistics. Each HSA is a collection of ZIP codes whose residents receive most of their hospitalizations from the hospitals in that area. HSAs are larger in rural areas than in urban areas to account for the fact that rural residents are likely to travel farther to access care. Block groups will receive the value for the HSA in which they are located.
source: Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems Patient survey (HCAHPS), downloaded August 2024

met_trans_fatal.label: Crash rate
met_trans_fatal.suffix: fatal crashes per 100,000 people per year
met_trans_fatal.definition: Annual average number of fatal crashes per 100,000 people; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This metric counts the number of fatal crashes within a 5-mile radius of the neighborhood’s population center to assess safety on the surrounding streets. Fatal crashes are relatively rare in any given neighborhood, so we use a 5-year average to control for year-to-year changes.

We then divide by the population in that 5-mile buffer and multiply by 100,000 to calculate the fatality rate.

The fatal crash rate is not the same as the fatality rate, as there may be multiple fatalities associated with a single crash.

We use statistical techniques to account for extremely high fatality rates in large geographic areas with low population.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Motor vehicle crashes are a leading cause of death in the U.S. Crashes occur most often in areas with high-speed limits or poorly designed streets, and in places where people must drive farther or more frequently to reach their destinations. Bicyclists and pedestrians are particularly vulnerable to crashes, as are children and older adults.
met_trans_fatal.results_comparable: No. The methodology changed in 2023. New statistical methods to account for extremely high outliers render approximately one-third of neighborhoods incomparable with earlier data years.
source: National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, 2018-2022 Fatality Analysis Reporting System

met_prox_activity.label: Activity density
met_prox_activity.suffix: jobs and people per sq. mi.
met_prox_activity.definition: Combined number of jobs and people per square mile measured: the Census Block scale, higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the combined residential and employment density of jobs and people in a neighborhood.
met_prox_activity.map_legend: Combined number of jobs and people per square mile
met_prox_activity.map_title: Combined number of jobs and people per square mile
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Generally speaking, the more compact a neighborhood, the less distance between residents and nearby jobs, businesses, or services. Compact neighborhoods make it easier to accomplish errands by foot, and make it more likely that neighbors will have the type of chance encounters that build community. To capture both of these benefits, the AARP Livability Index™ platform measures the combined density of jobs and people in a neighborhood.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Generally speaking, the more compact a neighborhood, the less distance between residents and nearby jobs, businesses, or services. Compact neighborhoods make it easier to accomplish errands by foot, and make it more likely that neighbors will have the type of chance encounters that build community. To capture both of these benefits, the Index measures the combined density of jobs and people in a neighborhood.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2022 Longitudinal Employer-Household Dynamics Origin-Destination Employment Statistics (LEHD LODES)

met_prox_sec.label: Crime rate
met_prox_sec.definition: Combined violent and property crimes per 10,000 people; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This metric measures the incidence of violent and property crimes, which are crimes with the greatest effect on personal safety, using the finest-scale nationwide data available.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

Data are unavailable for only two neighborhoods in the U.S. We assigned the average value for all Census block groups with data (281 crimes per 10,000) to Census block groups with missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

High crime rates make people feel unsafe and isolated in their own communities. Crime-free streets and public areas are a fundamental component of vibrant neighborhoods. Everyone deserves to live in an environment where they feel safe and comfortable socializing, exercising, or just hanging out in public.
source: FBI Uniform Crime Reports, as compiled by the National Archive of Criminal Justice Data, 2016

met_prox_vacant.label: Vacancy rate
met_prox_vacant.definition: Percentage of vacant housing units; lower values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform assesses the prevalence of vacant housing units in a particular geographic area.
missing_data:
__HTML__:

No missing data.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Highly livable neighborhoods are vibrant places that nurture a strong sense of community. A neighborhood with many vacant homes can indicate substandard or poorly maintained housing. Here, the Index measures the percentage of vacant housing units in a neighborhood.
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019-2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates

pol_prox_tod.label: State and local TOD programs
pol_prox_tod.definition: State and local programs that support transit-oriented development
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform recognizes state and local programs that support transit-oriented development. 

More specifically, the platform gives credit to states and communities with policy and programs that offer planning and technical assistance, zoning, infrastructure funding, land assembly, and tax incentives for TOD developers or businesses located near transit. 

Communities without local policy do not receive credit for state policy as TOD implementation is dependent on local action.  

Localities, and neighborhoods within them, receive credit for a regional policy or program.  

Our inventory is not comprehensive. If you believe your community has a TOD policy or program in place, please submit a link to it through our contact form https://livabilityindex.aarp.org/contact-us, and we will evaluate it for inclusion in the next update of the AARP Livability Index™ platform.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Transit-oriented development (TOD) creates walkable, diverse communities surrounding transit stations. These communities encourage people to take public transportation. TOD development can be costly and complex, which is why the platform gives credit to states and communities with programs that offer planning and technical assistance, infrastructure funding, land assembly, and tax incentives for TOD developers or businesses located near transit.
source: Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, December 2024

pol_house_visit.label: State and local inclusive design laws
pol_house_visit.definition: State and local laws that make housing accessible for people of all abilities
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The platform gives credit to state and local governments that have established mandatory or voluntary policies for new housing to be built with core accessibility features. Such features can include a zero-step entrance, wide doors and hallways, or a ground-floor bathroom.

State policies contribute only to a state’s score and not to scores at the city, county or neighborhood level. Local governments have authority over many aspects of housing policy, and state policies vary in terms of their strength and applicability. Therefore, it is not safe to assume that state policies will have a uniform effect on local creation of accessible housing.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The platform gives credit to state and local governments that have established mandatory or voluntary policies for new housing to be built with core accessibility features. Such features can include a zero-step entrance, wide doors and hallways, or a ground-floor bathroom.
rationale:
__HTML__:

As Americans live longer, homes built for easy access are becoming more necessary. At a minimum, a house should be “visitable” for someone in a wheelchair. Visitability requires features such as a zero-step entrance, wide doors and hallways, and a ground-floor bathroom.
source: Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, March 2025

pol_opp_credit.label: Local government creditworthiness
pol_opp_credit.definition: Local government AAA general obligation bond rating
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

S&P Global Ratings, an American financial research company, gives communities with the highest proven financial reliability a AAA rating, and the AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to cities and counties that have earned this rating.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Public investments such as parks, schools, roads, and transit all make communities livable, but they require substantial investment. Local governments often must borrow money and issue bonds to pay it back—but they need a good credit rating to do so. 

A low credit rating results in a higher cost to finance infrastructure projects, which, in turn, may take money away from key services like fire departments, schools, and older adults services.
source: S&P Global Ratings, July 2024

pol_env_connect.label: State utility disconnection policies
pol_env_connect.definition: State date-based policies prohibiting disconnection of utility service
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform awards credits to states with policies that prevent utilities from stopping service to any customer during seasons when extreme weather is likely. We credit states with date-based policies, providing consumers more predictability and peace of mind. States with temperature-based policies do not receive credit.  These policies benefit all residents of a state, thus all communities and neighborhoods in states with policy receive credit toward their local-level score.
rationale:
__HTML__:

In communities with harsh and unpredictable climates, reliable utilities are a must, especially for older adults. Even if customers are behind on their payments, supportive communities don’t disconnect key utilities during periods of exceptionally hot or cold weather.
source: U.S. Department of Health & Human Services Office of Community Services Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program, 2024 Seasonal Termination Protection Regulations

pol_engage_broad.label: State barriers to community broadband
pol_engage_broad.definition: Absence of state policies that prevent or discourage communities from operating public broadband networks
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states that allow community broadband networks to operate freely. 

Only state scores are affected by this policy. Localities and neighborhoods within those states do not receive credit toward their local score as local action must still be taken to create a community broadband network. Beginning with the 2025 version, states also receive additional score point at the state level - added after aggregation from the block group level - to ensure that the impact of such policies is reflected in their engagement score. Each state that is improved by this policy, one-seventh of a point is also added to the state’s overall score.
rationale:
__HTML__:

From students to grandparents to business owners, the internet provides people with information, connections, and opportunities they need to succeed. Many communities have created their own broadband networks that are directly accountable to local residents and businesses, but some states have enacted barriers that prevent or discourage communities from building these networks. This results in less competition among internet service providers and higher prices for consumers. Community broadband networks can help bridge the country’s digital divide and catalyze local economic development.
source: Institute for Local Self-Reliance Community Network Map August 2024

pol_trans_full_st.label: State and local Complete Streets policies
pol_trans_full_st.definition: State and local Complete Streets policies
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to any city, county, or state with a policy designed to offer pedestrians, cyclists, drivers, and transit users of all ages and abilities safe and convenient travel choices.  

All communities and neighborhoods in states with Complete Streets policies receive credit toward their local-level score. State transportation agencies are typically responsible for planning and designing the state highway system, which includes not only freeways, but also many main streets and commercial arterials. State Complete Streets policies can therefore have a major effect on the roads that are at the heart of local communities. 

Similarly, for regional policies, we give credit to the counties, towns, cities, and neighborhoods within each region, which we determine by reviewing the website for the regional agency administering the policy. In some cases, the geography listed covers a portion of a county. We awarded credit to counties that were only partially included in the jurisdiction of a Metropolitan Planning Organization with a Complete Streets policy.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Complete Streets policies require roads to be designed for safe, comfortable, and convenient travel by all means of travel—walking, biking, driving, and transit—and for all ages, abilities, and incomes.
