From wider sidewalks to new bike lanes to better intersection lighting, complete streets ensure easier and more inviting travel options.
source: The National Complete Streets Coalition (NCSC), a program of Smart Growth America, October 2024

pol_health_smoke.label: State and local smoke-free laws
pol_health_smoke.definition: State and local laws that prohibit smoking in workplaces, restaurants, and bars
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to any state or locality that bans smoking in workplaces, restaurants, and bars. We do not provide credit for locations that allow marijuana smoking in these locations. 

All communities and neighborhoods in states with policy receive credit toward their local-level score. However, not all county policies apply countywide. Some only apply to unincorporated portions of the county. For those policies we only provide credit to neighborhoods within those unincorporated areas.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Given the damage secondhand smoke can inflict, many states and localities prohibit smoking in public to protect their residents from unwanted health risks.
source: Tobacco control laws data were provided directly to us by the American Nonsmokers’ Rights Foundation U.S. Tobacco Control Laws Database, copyright © 2024, ANR Foundation

pol_engage_vote.label: State laws supporting voter participation
pol_engage_vote.definition: State laws allowing the following: all-mail and/or no-excuse absentee voting; adequate early voting; same-day voter registration; ballot “curing” procedures for absentee voters; automatic voter registration; and promoting voting access for people with disabilities.
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform awards credit to states that meet at least four of the following six criteria: 

  • All-mail and/or no-excuse absentee voting: States meet this criterion if they have all-mail voting, in which ballots are mailed to all registered voters instead of in-person voting. States that offer no-excuse absentee voting allow voters to request a mail-in ballot with no questions asked. 

  • Adequate early voting requires an early voting period of eight days or more (that is, more than one week). 

  • Automatic voter registration occurs when eligible individuals are automatically registered to vote while interacting with participating government agencies, such as the DMV. 

  • Same-day voter registration occurs when voters can both register and vote on Election Day and during the early voting period as well. 

  • Ballot “curing” procedures for absentee voters: States meet this criterion if they have statewide systems in place to notify voters when their ballot doesn’t have the required verification information and therefore will be rejected. Then, voters must be given an opportunity to fix, or cure, the error so that their ballot can be counted. A common example of an error is a missing signature or a signature that doesn’t match the one in the voter's record. 

  • Promoting voting access for people with disabilities: States meet this criterion when they pass laws or take statewide actions that go beyond minimum federal voting protections for voters with disabilities. 

Because these state laws typically impact local elections, policy credit is also awarded to communities and neighborhoods in states with this policy.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Election Day is typically held on a workday and may have limited hours and long lines, which can make it difficult for many people to exercise their right to vote. States can take many steps to increase voter participation, including an adequate early voting period of eight days or more prior to election day; no-excuse absentee voting, which allows voters to request a mail-in ballot no questions asked; or all-mail voting, which removes in-person voting altogether. 

In addition, states can promote voter participation by simplifying registration, eliminating deadlines and automatically registering voters. Same-day registration allows residents to register and vote at the same time on or until Election Day. Automatic voter registration registers eligible individuals to vote during routine interactions with government agencies. States can also promote voter engagement by improving accessibility for voters with disabilities. Further, states can ensure that each vote counts by giving voters an opportunity to correct ballot errors, when needed, by establishing statewide “curing” procedures.
source: National Conference of State Legislatures, State Profiles: Elections, February 2025

pol_trans_coord.label: State human services transportation coordination
pol_trans_coord.definition: State human services transportation coordination councils
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states that have established committees to coordinate service between transportation providers. 

States with regional coordinating committees that together serve the entire state also receive credit.  

All communities and neighborhoods in states with this policy in place receive credit toward their local-level score, given that transportation service providers in all cities and counties benefit from state coordinating councils.
rationale:
__HTML__:

A variety of organizations work to ensure that everyone has accessible transportation options. For example, an area agency on aging may provide van service to transport adults to activities at the local senior center, or the local department of health and human services may shuttle young adults to job training opportunities. Too often, however, services are fragmented, which can raise costs and reduce efficiency.  The existence of a statewide coordinating council can help remedy fragmented services.
source: Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, 2024

pol_env_hazard.label: Local multi-hazard mitigation plans
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to communities with current FEMA-approved multi-hazard mitigation plans that have been formally adopted by the local governing body or bodies, in the case of multi-jurisdictional plans. 

County-level plans, in some instances, only apply to the unincorporated portions of the county, thus only neighborhoods outside incorporated cities receive credit.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to communities with multi-hazard mitigation plans that are FEMA-approved and formally adopted by the local governing body.
rationale:
__HTML__:

While communities can’t prevent emergencies from happening, they can prepare for the worst to protect residents. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) pushes communities to develop mitigation plans that identify stakeholders, risks, and potential responses for a range of hazards like floods, tornadoes, and wildfires.
source: Federal Emergency Management Agency, July 2024 Hazard Mitigation Plan Status database

pol_house_trust.label: State and local housing trust funds
pol_house_trust.definition: State and local funds that support the development and preservation of affordable housing
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states, cities, and counties that have a housing trust fund in place.

State policies contribute only to a state’s score and not to scores at the city, county or neighborhood level. Although a state housing trust fund can support local affordable housing production, local governments must still take the initiative to provide affordable housing in order to benefit from a trust fund.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Housing trust funds allow communities to develop and preserve housing options for low-income residents. They are especially important for creating housing opportunities for people with lower incomes in areas where high demand drives up prices.
source: National Low Income Housing Coalition, Housing Trust Fund Project (data set updated as of September 27, 2024), and data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, May 2025

pol_opp_wage.label: State and local minimum wage increase
pol_opp_wage.definition: State and local minimum wage is higher than the federal minimum wage and is adjusted for increases in the cost of living
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states and localities that institute a minimum wage above the federal minimum and regularly—that is, for three years or more—adjust it upward to account for increases in the cost of living. 

Because these state laws benefit all workers, policy credit is also awarded to communities and neighborhoods in states with this policy. State or local government could also receive credit when the minimum wage is above the federal minimum wage and when the minimum wage has one or two planned increases that together amount to 25 percent or more of the current federal minimum wage. 

County policies that apply to unincorporated portions of a county only pass down credit to neighborhoods outside their incorporated cities and towns.
rationale:
__HTML__:

The current federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour—a rate that, for many workers, is inadequate to cover basic necessities such as food, housing, and medical care. Many families depend on second or third jobs. It’s important that communities ensure a living wage for all residents
source: The Economic Policy Institute’s “Minimum Wage Tracker”
UC Berkeley Labor Center, Inventory of US City and County Minimum Wage Ordinances

pol_env_eff.label: State energy efficiency scorecard
pol_env_eff.definition: State policies that support energy-efficient buildings, facilities, and appliances
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform awards credit to states that fall in the top quarter of ACEEE’s rankings. 

State energy efficiency policy benefits all residents within a state. All communities and neighborhoods in states that fall in the top quarter of ACEEE's rankings receive credit toward their local-level score.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE) ranks states based on a range of energy-efficient programs and policies, and the AARP Livability Index™ platform awards credit to states that fall in the top quarter of ACEEE’s rankings.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Energy efficiency initiatives protect the environment by minimizing pollution from fossil fuels. Green options like energy-optimized homes, appliances, and vehicles can also save people money on gas and electric bills. The American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy (ACEEE) ranks states based on a range of energy-efficient programs and policies.
source: ACEEE, 2025 State Energy Efficiency Scorecard

pol_trans_vol.label: State volunteer driver policies
pol_trans_vol.definition: State policies that remove barriers to volunteer driver programs
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This policy gives credit to states that prohibit one or more of the following actions that insurance companies could take based solely on serving as a volunteer driver: denying or canceling insurance, imposing a surcharge, or increasing rates

Almost every community has residents that rely on volunteer drivers, and these policies make it easier for volunteer drivers to help people, regardless of where they live within a state. Given this, all communities and neighborhoods in states with policy receive credit toward their local-level score.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Many people with restricted mobility rely on volunteer driver programs for an affordable and convenient way to get to the grocery store, doctor’s office, and other critical destinations.  

Those who don’t drive may rely on volunteer drivers to reach their destinations, and the need for volunteer drivers will likely increase as the population ages.  

In addition to driving, volunteers often help passengers walk or carry their packages. However, these programs face a common barrier: would-be volunteer drivers are deterred when insurance companies and agents tell them their car insurance rates may increase by serving as a volunteer driver.
source: Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, December 2024

pol_engage_right.label: Local human rights commissions
pol_engage_right.definition: Existence of a local human rights commission
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to cities and counties that have a local human rights commission in place. Data are available for 506 municipalities.
rationale:
__HTML__:

While federal law prohibits discrimination based on race, sex, age, or nationality, among other factors, many victims of discrimination lack the support they need to file a complaint. Cities and counties have increasingly established local human rights commissions that not only empower victims, but also take proactive steps to combat intolerance within the community. Some conduct education and outreach campaigns, advise local governments on key issues, or foster collaborative anti-discriminatory efforts.
source: Human Rights Campaign Foundation, Municipal Equality Index, November 2024

pol_opp_leave.label: State expansion of the Family and Medical Leave Act
pol_opp_leave.definition: State policies that expand upon the federal Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) to provide additional leave benefits to workers
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states that have expanded FMLA. Some expansion options include extending the duration of leave, covering lost wages, expanding coverage to smaller businesses and employees with shorter work histories, and extending FMLA to cover care for extended family members. For example, the federal FMLA does not cover grandparents, siblings, in-laws, or domestic partners. 

Because these state laws benefit all workers, policy credit is also awarded to communities and neighborhoods within states that have expanded FMLA.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Caring for oneself, parents, spouses, or other relatives is becoming the “new normal,” as Americans live longer. These responsibilities intensify the need for workers to have the option of taking extended time off to address a serious health condition or the birth or adoption of a child without sacrificing their job. That’s where FMLA comes in. It allows covered employees to take up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave.
source: Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, December 2024

pol_house_mfg.label: State manufactured housing protections
pol_house_mfg.definition: State laws guaranteeing notice and/or first right of purchase to residents of manufactured housing communities prior to sale
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states whose policies empower manufactured housing residents by requiring landowners to notify and grant residents first right of purchase before their community goes up for sale.  

State policies contribute only to a state’s score and not to scores at the city, county or neighborhood level. Since manufactured housing is typically located in rural areas and is not allowed by many local zoning codes, it is not safe to assume that this policy equally benefits all cities and counties in a state. 

Beginning with the 2025 version, states also receive additional score point at the state level - added after aggregation from the block group level - to ensure that the impact of such policies is reflected in their housing score. Each state that is improved by this policy, one-seventh of a point is also added to the state’s overall score.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Factory-built manufactured housing (or “mobile home”) communities provide economical housing options for lower-income families who may own their homes, but not the land underneath their homes. However, in most states, the land on which a manufactured housing community sits can be sold out from under the residents without giving them any advance notice or any opportunity to purchase the property.
source: National Consumer Law Center, 2024 List of State Manufactured Housing Laws

pol_house_foreclose.label: State foreclosure prevention and protection
pol_house_foreclose.definition: State policies and programs that protect homeowners from losing their homes to foreclosure
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to states that take at least two of these three actions to prevent and mitigate the impacts of foreclosure. 

All communities and neighborhoods in states with policy receive credit toward their local-level score. Foreclosures can affect communities throughout a state, and foreclosure prevention and protection programs can benefit any resident who is going through a foreclosure.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Foreclosures have devastating financial and economic consequences for homeowners and communities alike. To help minimize the risk and impact of foreclosures, states can (1) mediate foreclosures through judicial review, (2) abolish deficiency judgments that make homeowners liable for the balance of debt after the forced sale of their home, and (3) enable communities to manage foreclosed properties.
source: NOLO, 2024
Center for Community Progress, 2024

pol_engage_lgbt.label: Municipal LGBTQ+ anti-discrimination laws
pol_engage_lgbt.definition: Total score of 75 or greater from the Human Rights Campaign Municipal Equality Index
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The AARP Livability Index™ platform gives credit to cities and counties that receive a score of 75 or higher from the Human Rights Campaign Municipal Equality Index (MEI). 

The MEI rates 506 cities and counties on a scale of 0 to 100 on the basis of their inclusivity of Lesbian Gay Bisexual, Transgender, or Queer/Questioning (LGBTQ+) people who live and work there. The MEI covers five different issue areas:  

  • Nondiscrimination laws 

  • Municipality as employer 

  • Municipal services 

  • Law enforcement and 

  • Leadership on LGBTQ+ equality 

Factors related to LGBTQ+ rights include: relationship recognition, nondiscrimination laws, municipal employment practices, municipal services, law enforcement, and leadership commitment to full equality.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Since federal law doesn’t currently prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation, it’s up to state and local governments to protect equal rights for people who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, or queer or questioning (LGBTQ+). Some of the issues covered, such as reporting hate crimes, are relevant to non-LGBTQ+ residents as well and communities that are welcoming to the LGBTQ+ community tend to be more inclusive toward all residents and visitors.
source: Human Rights Campaign Foundation, Municipal Equality Index, November 2024

pol_house_adu.label: State accessory dwelling unit support
pol_house_adu.definition: State laws that facilitate the creation of local accessory dwelling units.
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This policy provides credit to states that have found ways to support and promote development of accessory dwelling units (ADUs). While the number of local policies is growing, no national comprehensive list exists. As such, this policy focuses only on state policy.

In general, all communities and neighborhoods within states with a policy in place receive credit for that state-level policy. The exceptions are Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Florida, Oregon, and Washington.

In Arizona, Connecticut, and Florida, the state laws are structured such that communities are not necessarily required to permit ADUs; therefore, credit is not extended to the community level.

In Colorado, Oregon, and Washington, the state laws require only certain communities that meet population-based and/or locational requirements to permit ADUs; therefore, credit is only extended to communities that meet those requirements. In these three states, credit is provided to the entirety of counties that meet these requirements.
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) are small, residential structures or units on the same property as detached single-family homes. This policy provides credit to states that have found ways to support and promote ADU development.
rationale:
__HTML__:

Accessory dwelling units (ADUs) are small residential units on the same property as detached single-family homes. Compared to traditional single-family home construction, ADUs can be a relatively lower-cost way to create flexible housing options for older adults and families alike. Despite increased popular interest and market conditions making many places ripe for ADU development, state and local laws and codes have not kept pace. In many jurisdictions, ADUs remain heavily restricted and regulated. As the need grows for more available and affordable housing, policymakers are looking for new ways to respond, and housing and zoning are particularly primed for action.
source: Joint Center for Housing Studies of Harvard University, Accessory Dwelling Units: Lessons for Massachusetts from Around the Country (2023)
Mercatus Center at George Mason University, A Taxonomy of State Accessory Dwelling Unit Laws (2023)
Data compiled by AARP Public Policy Institute, May 2025

pol_mult_age_friend.label: State and local commitment to create age-friendly communities
pol_mult_age_friend.definition: Communities that have taken comprehensive steps to prepare for the aging of the U.S. population
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

AARP gives credit to states and communities that have joined the AARP Network of Age-Friendly States and Communities or are otherwise members of the World Health Organization Global Network for Age-Friendly Cities and Communities.  

Although few states currently receive credit for this policy, those that do are working to improve statewide conditions for people of all ages. Therefore, localities and neighborhoods within age-friendly states receive credit toward their local scores.
rationale:
__HTML__:

By 2030, there will be twice as many Americans over the age of 65 as there were in 2000. To help residents live comfortably in all stages of life, communities must provide convenient transportation, walkable neighborhoods, affordable and accessible housing, multigenerational social opportunities, and inclusive business practices—just to name a few.
source: AARP Network of Age-Friendly States and Communities Member List (as of November 2023)

demo_pop.label: Total population
more_detail:
__HTML__:

In between censuses, the Census Bureau's Population Estimates Program produces and disseminates the official estimates of the population for the nation, states, counties, cities, and towns among other measures. We use the total population estimates on all available levels from the total population table with no additional calculations required.
demo_pop.scale: State, County, County Subdivision, Place, ZIP Code, Census Block Group
source: U.S. Census Bureau, 2019–2023 American Community Survey 5-Year Estimates
Zip code-level population data from Claritas, a proprietary data source.

demo_african.label: Percent Black or African American
demo_african.definition: Percent of the population that identifies as Black or African American
more_detail:
__HTML__:

Using the Census population and demographics estimates, specifically the "Race" 5-year estimates table, we obtain the number of people that identify as Black or African American, as well as the estimates of the total population on every available summary level. We use these two variables for our measure by dividing the number of people that identify as Black or African American by the total population on the same summary level to obtain the percentage of people that identify as Black or African American on that level.
demo_african.scale: State, County, County Subdivision, Place, Census Block Group

demo_up_mobile.label: Upward mobility
demo_up_mobile.definition: Average individual income for those in their mid-thirties who grew up with low-income parents (calculated for the neighborhood where they grew up), divided by the commuting-zone average individual income of those in their mid-thirties (regardless of parent income), then multiplied by 100 for better readability; higher values are better
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

This ratio is a measure of generational economic advantage/disadvantage. A value lower than 100 percent indicates some degree of disadvantage for those who grew up with low-income parents relative to their peers from the same metro area who grew up in higher income families. 

We assign income at age 35 to the neighborhood where they grew up, not to the neighborhood where they live today. Low-income is defined as being below the 25th percentile of incomes in the national distribution.

We report averages; we do not suggest that every individual’s economic outcome is preordained or determined. The data do, however, suggest that targeted investments in schools, housing, job access, and quality health care in these disadvantaged neighborhoods could help address economic inequality in the U.S.

disaster_natural_hazard_risk.label: Natural Hazard Risk
disaster_natural_hazard_risk.definition: A community’s relative exposure to natural hazards. This score accounts for the frequency and severity of hazards, expected annual losses, social vulnerability, and community resilience.
interpretation_notes:
__HTML__:

The FEMA National Risk Index (NRI) is a dataset and tool developed by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to help communities understand their relative risk to 18 natural hazards, such as hurricanes, earthquakes, and wildfires. It combines data on hazard frequency and severity with social vulnerability, community resilience, and expected annual losses to generate an overall risk score for U.S. counties, census tracts, and other geographic units.

To make the raw risk values easier to interpret, an algorithm (k-means clustering) is used to group them into five categories, ranging from very low to very high. This clustering is done separately for each geographic level—for example, all counties are grouped together, and all census tracts are grouped together.

Because of this, locations with the same raw risk value—or even places that cover the same area but are reported at different geographic levels—may end up with different risk ratings. This is because the grouping is based on how a location’s risk value compares to others within the same geographic level, not across all areas.
source: FEMA National Risk Index (NRI)
